The provisions of section 186(2) of the Act read with the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) 
Rules, 2014, inter-alia, provides that no company is permitted to, directly or indirectly, (a) give any 
loan to any person or other body corporate; (b) give any guarantee or provide security in connection 
with a loan to any other body corporate or person; and (c) acquire by way of subscription, purchase or 
otherwise, the securities of any other body corporate, exceeding:  
 
(i) 
sixty percent of its paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium account; or  
(ii) 
one hundred per cent of its free reserves and securities premium account, whichever is more.  
 
The sub-section (3) of section 186 of the Act provides that advancing of any loan or guarantee or 
providing any security or the acquisition as provided under section 186(2) of the Act, exceeds the limits 
specified therein, a prior approval of members by means of a Special Resolution is required. The first 
proviso to section 186(3) of the Act provides that where a loan or guarantee is advanced or where a has 
security been provided by a company to its wholly owned subsidiary company or a joint venture 
company, or acquisition is made by a holding company, by way of subscription, purchase or otherwise 
of, the securities of its wholly owned subsidiary company, the requirement of 186(3) of the Act shall 
not apply. As per explanation to section 2(87) of the Act, for the purpose of definition of “subsidiary 
company”, the expression “company” includes any body corporate.  
 
Further, sub-section (11) of section 186 of the Act provides for certain exemptions to certain categories 
of companies for certain types of transaction from applicability of section 186 of the Act. In this respect, 
section 186(11)(b)(i) of the Act exempts any investment made by an investment company from 
applicability of provisions of section 186 of the Act. The explanation to sub-section (13) of section 186 
of the Act defines an ‘investment company’ to mean “a company whose principal business is the 
acquisition of shares, debentures or other securities and a company will be deemed to be principally 
engaged in the business of acquisition of shares, debentures or other securities, if its assets in the form 
of investment in shares, debentures or other securities constitute not less than fifty per cent of its total 
assets, or if its income derived from investment business constitutes not less than fifty per cent as a 
proportion of its gross income”. The members may note that as on March 31, 2026, assets in the form 
of investment in shares, debentures or other securities constitutes more than 50% of the total assets of 
the Company.  
 
Further, in terms of Regulation 23 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations 
and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI Listing Regulations”), all related party 
transactions, including material related party transactions, require prior approval of the Audit 
Committee and the shareholders of the Company, as applicable, unless otherwise exempted under the 
afore-mentioned Regulations. Considering that the transactions contemplated under this Item involve 
grant of loans, guarantees, securities and/or investments in excess of the thresholds prescribed under 
applicable law and may involve transactions with related parties other than wholly owned subsidiaries, 
the Board, as a matter of good corporate governance, transparency and in compliance with the SEBI 
Listing Regulations, considers it appropriate to seek the approval of the members by way of a Special 
Resolution. 
 
The members may note that the permissible limits under subsection (2) of section 186 of the Act, for 
intercorporate loan, provide guarantee(s) or security(s), or investment(s) by the Company as on March 
31, 2026, is INR 367,571 million. 
 
Considering the various strategic acquisitions, organic and inorganic growth by the Company, the 
Company has already made loan, provided guarantee or security and subscribed to the securities to the 
tune of INR 591,880 million as on March 31, 2026. The afore-mentioned amount of includes loans, 
guarantee or security and/or investments made to wholly owned subsidiary companies (“WOS”) to the 
tune of INR 514,120 million as on March 31, 2026, which are exempted under first proviso to sub-
section (3) of section 186 of the Act, from requirement of obtaining prior shareholders’ approval. 
Further, as on March 31, 2026, the loans, guarantee, security investment etc. in legal entities or other 
person, i.e. other than Joint Venture(s) and WOS which are exempted under sub-section (3) of section 
186 of the Act, is INR 77,759 million.

t was among the more demanding operating 
environments our industry has faced in recent 
decades, and yet Motherson delivered record

the resilience and the architecture of the business we have built 
together over many years.
I will take you through the details of our performance in the pages 
that follow. Before turning to the numbers, I want to oﬀer a 
reflection: businesses are ultimately tested not under benign 
conditions but in adversity. FY26 was that test for Motherson - 
and the result fills me with confidence, not just in what we have 
achieved, but in what we are capable of achieving in the years

Financial performance 
I am pleased to share that, for the first time in Motherson’s history, 
consolidated revenues crossed the INR 1.25 trillion threshold in 
FY26. Our topline grew by a healthy 11% year-on-year, a meaningful 
achievement in a tough operating environment. EBITDA growth was 
equally encouraging, rising in tandem with revenues to INR 120.3 
billion, once again showing that when our revenues grow, our 
diversified model lets profits grow right alongside them.
Profit after tax attributable to our shareholders rose to INR 38.6 
billion - a number that reflects not just commercial success, but 
that we are creating real value for every rupee you have 
entrusted to us.
Our booked busines

s stands at USD 96.0 billion, providing 
exceptional revenue visibility for the near-to medium-term. 
Equally encouraging is the state of our balance sheet: net
leverage has reached an all-time low of 0.8x, reflecting disciplined 
capital allocation and strong cash generation. This strong balance 
sheet provides us with strategic headroom so that when the right 
acquisition opportunity comes, we can move quickly.

FY26 marked an important step in Motherson’s journey towards 
becoming a truly diversified, multi-industry enterprise. Our 
strategic expansion beyond automotive continues to gain 
momentum, with steady progress across our non-automotive 
businesses. These businesses have matured beyond their early 
stages and are beginning to make meaningful contributions to 
both revenue and margins, strengthening our growth.
Our consumer electronics business delivered strong momentum 
this financial year, achieving 7.5x growth and turning EBITDA 
positive in its very first full year of operations. This performance 
reflects the strength of Motherson’s proven operational 
capabilities – speed, scale, and quality – when we apply them to 
an adjacent, fast-moving industry. In aerospace, we registered 
40% year-on-year growth, achieving 10x growth over the past 
three years. These outcomes reflect the steady and disciplined 
execution of a diversification strategy that we have been building 
over the past several years.
Underpinning this progress is our proven D.E.M.A.L. framework 
– our capability to Design, Engineer, Manufacture, Assemble, and 
manage Logistics of complex products across multiple industries
and geographies. This is the foundation on which our 
diversification rests, and I am delighted by what our teams have 
built.

O

ur Vision 2030 goals remain our north star, and I am glad to 
report that we continue to make meaningful progress against 
each of the pillars we have committed to.
Group revenues advanced from USD 21.2 billion to USD 22.9 
billion this year. The journey to our USD 108 billion revenue target 
is long, but every step we have taken is aimed at it. Our booked 
business, the breadth of our new business wins, and the depth of 
our customer relationships all give me confidence that we are 
moving in the right direction to achieve our ambitions.
Return on Capital Employed moderated this year, as discussed. 
However, the 40% ROCE target remains firmly in place for each 
business unit, and our investments continue to be disciplined and 
aligned to achieve this. We remain focused on creating 
sustainable long-term value and do not compromise long-term 
returns for short-term considerations.

embedded in our portfolio over the years. When individual

last

extraordinarily diﬀicult period for the automotive industry 
globally. Commodity inflation on a scale rarely witnessed 
before has squeezed margins across the value chain. Several 
of the world’s largest automakers found themselves navigating 
the consequences of electric-vehicle strategies that did not 
unfold as anticipated. Geopolitical tensions disrupted trade 
routes and supply chains. Tariﬀ regimes shifted. Government 
subsidies – which had been a significant tailwind for EV 
adoption in certain markets – were withdrawn or curtailed, 
dampening demand.
And yet, in the face of all this, Motherson recorded its best-ever 
financial performance. This is the result of years of deliberate 
work and ongoing eﬀorts to build a company that is resilient – 
diversified by customer, product, geography, and now, 
increasingly, by industry.
As the industry finds its footing in the post-disruption 
environment, as our new businesses continue to scale, and as the 
full benefits of our record capital investments begin to flow 
through, I believe Motherson is well-positioned for tremendous 
growth in the coming years. Our Vision 2030 targets are goals 
that our teams are working towards with rigour, grit, and a sense 
of shared purpose.

revenue, no single customer more than 10%, 
and no single component more than 10%. 
This diversiﬁcation is our most important

emerging markets continue to ﬁre. Emerging

OEMs move faster or slower toward 
electriﬁcation, we supply across ICE, hybrid, 
and EV platforms. This posture has been an 
important diﬀerentiator in a year when several 
large OEMs recalibrated their EV timelines. 
Our booked business as of FY26 stood at USD 
96.0 billion, reﬂecting customer trust across 
powertrain types.
Increasing content per vehicle has been 
another key driver. As vehicles become more 
complex – whether through advanced driver

systems, or premium interiors – Motherson’s 
wallet share per unit increases even when 
overall volumes are ﬂat. Over and above this, 
inorganic growth through disciplined

Q4
Despite high capex 
and continued 
acquisitions, 
leverage is at an all-time low. How 
do you view leverage going 
forward?
We improved our net leverage ratio to 0.8x 
Net Debt to EBITDA in FY26 – an all-time low 
– even as we execute

d the highest capex in 
our history and completed multiple 
acquisitions. This is not a coincidence; it 
reﬂects a ﬁnancial philosophy that has been 
consistently applied over many years.
For over a decade, Motherson has maintained 
a stated policy of keeping leverage below 
2.5x. Internally, our target is closer to 1.5x, 
because we want to preserve the ﬁnancial 
ﬂexibility to act decisively when strategic 
opportunities arise. Operating at 0.8x gives us 
signiﬁcant headroom.
The improvement in leverage, despite active 
investments, was due to three disciplines 
operating simultaneously. First, strong internal 
accruals. Our business generates healthy 
operating cash ﬂows, and these are the 
primary fuel for our investment activity. 
Finance cost declined year-on-year by
14% in FY26, reﬂecting the improving quality 
of our balance sheet.
Second, capex eﬀiciency. As mentioned, we 
only invest when we have ﬁrm customer 
orders. This discipline shortens the time 
between spend and revenue, so capital does 
not sit idle for long. Our 13 active growth 
capex projects across emerging markets are 
all tied to speciﬁc customer commitments 
with deﬁned ramp-up schedules.
Third, acquisition quality. We are disciplined 
about valuations. We do not pursue scale for 
its own sake.

Passenger vehicle 
market growth in 
developed 
economies continued to face

The slowdown in developed market 
passenger vehicle volumes has been real and 
has had a visible impact on our growth rate in 
those geographies. The EV transition in 
Europe and North America did not play out as 
originally planned by OEMs – consumer 
adoption was s

lower than forecast, regulatory 
timelines shifted, and many large OEMs 
scaled back or deferred signiﬁcant portions of 
their EV investment programmes. This 
recalibration created uncertainty in the supply 
chain, including for Motherson.
However, this story is beginning to turn. 
During FY26, most major European OEMs 
restructured their investment programmes 
and are now aligned with more realistic 
timelines for the powertrain transition. 
Critically, the FY27 model launch pipeline 
from these OEMs is among the largest in 
years – for some, a record. New model 
launches are consistently our biggest growth 
trigger, as fresh platforms come with higher 
content requirements and often bring us new 
business wins. Motherson has a meaningful 
share of business across several of these 
upcoming platforms, which positions us well 
for FY27 and beyond.
Also, our exposure has become signiﬁcantly 
more balanced than it was a few years ago. 
The deliberate diversiﬁcation we have 
pursued – into emerging markets, into 
Chinese OEMs that are rapidly expanding 
their global exports, into non-automotive 
businesses – means that a soft year in Europe 
or North America no longer creates a 
disproportionate drag on our consolidated 
performance. India and ASEAN delivered 
strong growth in FY26. Our Consumer 
Electronics and Aerospace businesses are 
growing at rates that far exceed the 
automotive cycle.
Looking ahead, global LV production is 
expected to grow from approximately 92 
million units in FY26 to around 93 million units 
in FY27. Combined with the launch pipeline, 
the improving macro picture in Europe, and 
our own share gains, we are optimistic about 
our growth trajectory going into FY27.

and geo-political 
uncertainty have

Motherson navigating these risks?
Commodity costs and geo-political risks are 
perhaps the most consistent operational 
challenges in our industry, and FY26 has been 
no diﬀerent. Copper pr

ices rose by ~38% over 
FY25, a trend directly relevant to our wiring 
harness business. Resin prices, which aﬀect 
our Modules & Polymer Products division, 
have been inﬂuenced by crude oil price 
movements linked to developments in the 
Middle East. The Group has pass-through 
arrangements with its major customers for 
raw material price variations, which are 
actualised periodically. These arrangements 
are not instantaneous – there can be a 
settlement lag of one to two quarters – but 
they provide structural protection over the 
medium-term.
We also have a dedicated Global Sourcing 
and Procurement team which enables us to 
leverage our purchasing volumes across 
geographies to negotiate better terms, build 
deeper supplier relationships, and reduce 
exposure to spot market volatility.

India’s trade agreement activity in the past

positive, even if some of the beneﬁts will 
materialise over a multi-year horizon.
The India–EU FTA, concluded in January 2026, 
is the most consequential of these 
agreements given the concentration of global 
OEMs in Europe. For the automotive sector, 
the headline provision is the phased 
reduction of duties on European cars from 
110% to 10%. Even duties on automotive 
components will be fully phased out over ﬁve 
to ten years.
The India–EU FTA will beneﬁt Motherson in 
many ways. First, our European OEM 
customers – who are the largest component 
of our client base – stand to beneﬁt from 
expanded Indian market access, which 
should support their India investment plans 
and increase volumes for our Indian 
operations. Second, the zero-duty access for 
Indian auto components into EU markets 
enhances the export competitiveness of our 
Indian manufacturing base, which supplies 
globally. Third, as European OEMs deepen 
their manufacturing presence in India in 
response to the FTA, Motherson, as a locally

Q9
Aerospace has 
grown rapidly and is 
increasingly being 
seen as a strategic growth vertical. 
What is the long-term vision?
Aerospace is another clear demonstration of 
how Motherson’s strategy of leveraging its 
core engineering and manufacturing 
capabilities into adjacent high-growth sectors 
can create signiﬁcant value. Three years ago, 
this was a nascent business. Today, it is a 
meaningful contributor with a clearly deﬁned 
growth runway.
In FY26, the Aerospace business delivered 
40% year-on-year revenue growth, continuing 
a trajectory in which our top-line in this 
segment has expanded approximately 10x 
over the past three years. The order book 
grew 20%+ year-on-year to USD 1.6 billion, 
providing strong multi-year revenue visibility. 
This is signiﬁcant – aerospace contracts are 
long-duration by nature, which means this 
order book translates into a predictable and 
growing revenue stream over the next several 
years.
During the year, we expanded our product 
portfolio across multiple platforms. We 
secured orders for metallic parts, sub-
assemblies and wiring harnesses in business 
jets and rotary-wing aircraft, adding to our 
existing capabilities in ﬁxed-wing commercial 
platforms. This diversiﬁcation across 
segments – commercial aviation and 
business aviation – mirrors the multi-
customer and multi-segment strategy that 
has served us well in automotive, and for 
similar reasons: it reduces concentration risk 
and opens multiple avenues for growth.
What makes Motherson well-suited to 
Aerospace is not just our manufacturing 
scale, but our compliance capabilities. 
Aerospace demands extremely high-quality 
standards, rigorous certiﬁcation processes, 
and long-term relationship management with 
OEMs – all of which are core competencies 
we have reﬁned over decades in the 
automotive industry. We are deepening our 
engagement with existing customers and 
actively pursuing n

ew programme wins, 
which should continue to expand both our 
content and our customer base.
Strategically, we see Aerospace as one of the 
principal drivers of Motherson’s non-
automotive revenue growth toward our Vision 
2030 targets. The combination of a growing 
global ﬂeet and the shift toward lighter and 
more electronically complex aircraft – all of 
which increases the complexity and value of 
the systems we supply – makes this a 
compelling long-term opportunity for us.

FY26 has been one of the most challenging and 
consequential years for the global automotive 
industry in recent memory. The year was shaped 
not by a single disruptive event but by a 
convergence of structural forces and acute shocks 
– US trade tariﬀs that fundamentally reordered 
global supply chains, a major geopolitical conflict in
the Middle East that disrupted energy and logistics 
markets, persistent commodity cost pressure, and 
the continued – if uneven – march of vehicle 
electrification.
US Trade Tariﬀs: A structural realignment of 
the supply chain
The single most consequential development for the global 
automotive supply chain for the majority of FY26 has been the 
imposition of sweeping US trade tariﬀs under Section 232 of the 
Trade Expansion Act. Beginning 03 April 2025, a 25% tariﬀ took 
eﬀect on imported automobiles and a broa

d set of automotive 
parts – including engines, transmissions, powertrain 
components, and electrical systems. A separate 25% tariﬀ on 
steel and aluminium imports also came into force. A baseline 
tariﬀ of 10% on goods from all countries, with higher reciprocal 
levies on select markets, added further layering to the cost 
environment. The tariﬀ regime was subsequently extended in 
October 2025 to cover medium and heavy-duty vehicles (25%) 
and buses (10%), with USMCA-compliant imports receiving 
partial or conditional relief. An import adjustment oﬀset of 3.75% 
of aggregate vehicle MSRP was made available to 
US-assembling OEMs for a transitional period, declining to 2.5% 
from May 2026.
The financial toll on the global automotive industry has been 
significant. OEMs globally have collectively absorbed billions of 
dollars in tariﬀ-related costs, with several announcing 
meaningful earnings downgrades. For Tier-1 suppliers and 
component manufacturers, the impact has been two-
directional: direct cost escalation for goods exported to the US 
market, and indirect pressure through OEM production 
adjustments, sourcing realignments, and the accelerated 
reshoring of assembly activities to the United States. The tariﬀ 
structure has also introduced the concept of ‘stacking’ – where 
components crossing multiple borders accumulate cumulative 
duty exposure – increasing complexity in cost modelling and 
customer pricing negotiations. We are relatively well placed to

evolution and actively managing energy procurement, supply 
chain rerouting, and customer communication to minimise

Commodity input costs: Structurally elevated,
tariﬀ-distorted
Commodity markets in FY26 have been characterised by 
structurally elevated prices, significantly compounded by both 
tariﬀ-driven distortions and, in the latter part of the year, supply 
disruptions arising from the Iran conflict. Aluminium prices, 
which began FY26 at around mid-USD 2,500s per tonne, 
trended higher throughout the year, approaching USD 2,900 
per tonne by year-end, driven by China’s maintained production 
capacity ceiling, shrinking global inventories, and strong 
demand from the automotive, solar, and grid sectors. The Iran 
conflict has added a new and acute dimension, with Gulf-based 
aluminium capacity curtailed and European manufacturers 
facing surging energy input costs. Copper prices have similarly 
trended toward record nominal highs, with analysts expecting 
average prices between USD 11,000 - USD 14,000 per tonne in 
CY 2026, supported by persistent supply-demand imbalances, 
depleted exchange inventories, and the structural

pull of 
electrification on demand.
The tariﬀ environment has further distorted commodity trade 
flows, creating local price spikes and procurement complexity. 
Early in the fiscal year, the threat of US Section 232 tariﬀs on 
copper imports triggered a sharp premium of COMEX prices 
over the LME, drawing physical copper inventories into the US 
and creating temporary shortages elsewhere. The 25% US tariﬀ 
on steel and aluminium has increased eﬀective input costs for 
US-sourced materials and incentivised inventory pre-
positioning. We continue to pursue cost pass-through 
arrangements with our customers, deepen procurement 
diversification, and explore product-level engineering 
optimisation to manage the impact of elevated and volatile 
input costs.

environment
The macroeconomic backdrop for FY26 has been shaped by a 
significant divergence in trajectory across our major operating 
regions, with the Iran conflict emerging as a late-year 
complication to central bank policy in several economies.

India has been

a standout performer. Real GDP grew 7.7% in FY26 
– among the fastest in recent years – driven by resilient domestic 
consumption, a healthy monsoon, fiscal stimulus through 
frontloaded capital expenditure, and the disinflationary benefit of 
food price correction and GST rationalisation. The Reserve Bank 
of India reduced the policy repo rate by a cumulative 100 basis 
points through the year, bringing it to 5.25% by December 2025, 
and held it at that level at the April and June 2026 meetings, 
assessing the impact of earlier cuts in a context of improving 
growth and benign inflation. Full-year CPI inflation for FY26 stood 
at 2.1%, a historic low, with FY27 CPI inflation projected upwards at 
5.1% in the wake of commodity and energy inflation, still and well 
within the RBI’s medium-term target band of 2%–6%. The RBI has 
revised India’s FY27 GDP growth forecast to 6.6%. This 
environment is supportive of domestic vehicle demand, 
consumer financing, and investment activity, though the Iran 
conflict introduces some upward risk to energy prices and the 
current account.
In the United States, the Federal Reserve cut rates three times in 
the second half of calendar year 2025, reducing the federal funds 
rate to a range of 3.50%–3.75% by December 2025 - a cumulative 
reduction of 175 basis points from the September 2024 peak. The 
Fed held rates steady at its January, March and April 2026 
meetings, adopting a wait-and-see stance as it assessed the 
inflationary impact of rising oil prices following the conflict in Iran. 
Core PCE inflation is now expected to be 2.7% in CY 2026, above 
the 2% target.
In the European Union, the ECB completed eight rate cuts from 
June 2024 to June 2025, bringing the deposit rate to 2.0%. 
However, at its June 2026 meeting, the ECB raised rates by 25 
bps to 2.25% citing renewed inflationary pressures due to the 
Middle East conflict. The ECB has reiterated a data-dependent 
and meeting-by-meeting approach as it assesses the evolv

ing 
inflation and growth trajectories across the Eurozone.

light vehicle sales. For financial year 2026, BEV sales grew by 
approximately 22% to around 16.9 million units, representing close 
to 18.4% of global sales – an improvement in the rate of growth,

Supply chain resilienc

e under renewed stress
The supply chain environment has deteriorated meaningfully in 
the second half of FY26, after a period of relative stabilisation 
earlier in the year. The most acute new disruption has come 
from the Iran conflict, which has closed or substantially 
restricted access to the Strait of Hormuz – a critical node in 
global maritime trade through which significant volumes of 
automotive parts, raw materials, and finished vehicles transit. 
Shipping insurers have increased premiums on Gulf routes, 
logistics companies are rerouting cargo, and freight costs on 
aﬀected lanes have risen sharply. For the automotive supply 
chain, which relies heavily on just-in-time delivery, extended 
transit times and route uncertainty add meaningful inventory 
and cost risk.
Earlier in the year, the tariﬀ environment introduced a diﬀerent 
form of supply chain stress: the risk of ‘tariﬀ stacking’ on 
crossborder component flows, pressure on USMCA 
compliance and content documentation, and a strategic 
impetus among OEMs to accelerate US manufacturing 
localisation. These dynamics have prompted a structural 
rethink of global network design, with resilience and 
robustness increasingly displacing pure cost optimisation as 
the primary criterion. Alongside these macro disruptions, a 
second-order semiconductor tightness also emerged in 2025, 
arising from a trade standoﬀ aﬀecting Netherlands-based 
chipmakers – a reminder that electronics supply chains remain 
structurally fragile. In our own operations, we have continued 
to strengthen supplier diversification, build inventory buﬀers 
for critical materials, and deploy multi-modal logistics 
solutions. The conflict in Iran reinforces our commitment to 
maintaining supply continuity for our customers as an absolute 
operational priority.
OEM industry stress and supplier landscape
The financial health of the global automotive industry has 
diverged sharply between OEMs and suppliers in FY26. OEMs 
have borne the brunt

of stagnant volumes, elevated input 
costs, tariﬀ exposure, and the capital demands of the 
electrification transition, with a considerable decline in their 
EBITDA margins. This compression has led to OEM production 
adjustments, model launch deferrals, and intensified pressure 
on supplier pricing. Automotive supplier distress metrics have, 
however, shown some improvement, with the share of 
suppliers in financial distress declining from approximately 31% 
in CY 2024 to approximately 24% in CY 2025, supported by 
eﬀective cost management and pricing discipline. M&A activity 
in the supplier sector has rebounded after historic lows in CY 
2024, with deal volume increasing – particularly in the 
powertrain and electronics segments – as companies seek 
scale, technology alignment, and portfolio rationalisation. For 
us, this environment requires heightened customer 
engagement, transparent cost discussions, and a focus on the 
product categories where our value proposition is most 
diﬀerentiated.
Climate policy and ESG mandates
Sustainability regulation and ESG disclosure requirements 
continued to gain ground in FY26, though the pace and 
certainty of regulatory transition have become more 
geographically uneven. In the EU, the broader political debate 
around the achievability of 2035 ICE phase-out timelines is 
prompting recalibration, with the automotive package 
discussion centring on a more technology-inclusive path to 
decarbonisation. Despite this, mandatory ESG disclosure 
requirements under frameworks such as CSRD are expanding 
the scope of sustainability reporting across the value chain, 
including for suppliers. The Iran conflict, paradoxically, may 
accelerate the momentum toward electrification in some 
markets as consumers and policymakers respond to energy 
price volatility. In India, the government’s PLI scheme, green 
manufacturing incentives, and EV ecosystem investment are 
reshaping procurement strategies and influencing OEM 
sourcing decisions

. For us, alignment with customer’s  
decarbonisation goals, ESG compliance across markets, and 
investment in energy eﬀiciency and renewable sourcing 
remain integral to long-term competitiveness and customer 
relationship management.

deliver consistent value at scale.

Bolstering the balance sheet with capital raise
In June 2025, SAMIL raised INR 20,250 million by way of Listed, 
Unsecured, Redeemable, Non-Convertible Debentures (“NCDs”) 
on a private placement basis, allotted on June 27, 2025, with 
maturity date as 27 June 2030. The raised capital has been 
majorly utilised for refinancing the existing debt, keeping the 
net debt level stable while optimising the cost of capital. The 
net leverage ratio at the end FY26 stands at 0.8x, well within the 
Group’s defined policy of 2.5x. 
Progressing on sustainable journey
Aimed at achieving carbon neutrality by 2040, the Group has 
been sustainably investing in a phased renewable transition 
strategy based on consumption and emissions priorities 
across key regions, with a special focus on India. In FY26, 
SAMIL invested in the following projects: 
(i) Captive PPA - 50 MWp Captive Solar Plant in Tamil Nadu, 
reducing carbon emissions by ~1.38 MMT over project life
(ii) Investing in ~15 MWp Captive Solar Project in Uttar 
Pradesh, reducing carbon emissions by 0.23 MMT over
project life 
Financial discipline and outlook
The Group’s financial framework remains anchored in 
disciplined capital allocation, proactive working 
capital management, and a focus on free cash flow 
generation. During FY26, the net leverage ratio 
remained stable, and the Group maintained ample 
liquidity to fund both organic investments and the 
acquisitions pipeline. Continuous improvement 
initiatives - including monitoring and turning around 
underperforming units, optimising working capital 
operationally, enhancing eﬀiciencies, and realising 
Group synergies – remain embedded in the 
management cadence across all business divisions.

Risk Management 
The Group has a global presence and decentralised management 
structure. During the financial year 2025 –26, the Group navigated 
a complex operating environment marked by persistent internal 
and external challenges. Macroeconomic uncertainties and 
geopolitical developments continued to influence the Group’s 
overall risk landscape throughout the year. At the macro level, the 
Group is exposed to risks associated with global organisations 
and the automotive industry in particular. Eﬀectively mitigating 
risks from all directions is one of the challenges that the Group 
targets. Risk is an inherent component of business growth and 
strategic decision making, but not all risks are not equal. Risk 
mitigation eﬀorts are calibrated according to the likelihood of 
exposure and the potential downside of an incident. The Group is 
exposed to various risks within each of its business segments and 
products. 
Risk Management structure
The first step for risk management is in creating an eﬀective risk 
management system is to understand the qualitative distinctions 
among the types of risks that organisations face. The Board of 
Directors of a legal entity are responsible for risk oversight under 
applicable laws The Board of

Directors has set up a Risk 
Management Committee, (“RMC”) to periodically, inter-alia, review 
Operating Risks, Regulatory Risks, Strategic RisksCyber Security 
Risks amongst others in the business and their mitigating factors. 
RMC periodically review the risk(s) and their mitigation strategies 
for all of its subsidiaries and joint ventures. The risk management 
and mitigation strategies are governed by a structured, multi-
layered oversight mechanism:
•
Board of Directors: Holds ultimate oversight and 
responsibility for framing and monitoring the risk 
management plan, ensuring that risk mitigation is 
embedded in all aspects of operations and strategy under 
the framework assessed by the management in the business 
environment under which it operates. 
•
Risk Management Committee (RMC): A dedicated 
committee at the board level oversees the risk management 
process. The Committee review on periodic basis risk 
assessment, evaluation and mitigation steps taken by the 
management team including the Chief Risk Oﬀicers (CRO) 
of respective business.

1.
Risk Identification
Each business division conducts systematic reviews to 
identify and understand risks across three dimensions:
•
Risk identification :raising awareness and building 
capability across all teams to recognise risk indicators 
early.
•
Probability evaluation :assessing the likelihood that an 
identified risk will materialise within a given timeframe.
•
Consequence evaluation :determining the impact and 
potential financial losses to establish the size and 
priority of each risk.
2.
 Risk Measurement
Risks are evaluated and scored on approved parameters to 
determine their significance and priority:
•
Impact classification : rated as Extreme, Moderate or 
Minor based on eﬀect on financial performance, credit 
rating, market share, regulatory prosecution and fines 
and and health safety issues to employees and third 
parties.
•
Likelihood classification : assessed as Frequent, Likely 
or Unlikely based on historical data, expert judgement 
and forward-looking indicators.
•
Risk impact matrix : combining impact and likelihood 
ratings to produce a composite risk scor

e that drives 
prioritisation decisions.
3.
 Risk Examination
Identified and measured risks are examined in depth to 
determine the most eﬀective response strategy:
•
Review of available mitigation options, existing 
controls and gap areas requiring new or enhanced 
measures.
•
Assessment of remediation approaches including risk 
acceptance, transfer, avoidance or reduction 
strategies.
•
Alignment of proposed responses with business 
continuity and contingency planning requirements.
4.
 Risk Implementation
Selected controls and mitigation actions are formally 
executed with clear ownership and governance:
•
Deployment of approved controls and remediation 
measures across relevant business divisions and 
functions.
•
Assignment of named accountability to responsible 
owners with defined timelines and deliverables.
•
Integration with business continuity and contingency 
planning to ensure operational preparedness and 
protection of personnel and assets.
5.
 Risk Monitoring
A continuous monitoring mechanism ensures controls 
remain eﬀective and risks are managed on an ongoing basis:
•
Ongoing tracking of implemented measures against 
defined effectiveness criteria and performance 
indicators.
•
Structured reporting of outcomes on a defined review 
cycle to senior management and relevant governance 
bodies.

back into the Identification stage to ensure the risk register

Based on analysis and evaluation, RMC assesses various risks in 
the following categories:
1.
Strategic Risks: This includes risks with respect to new 
business opportunities, Mergers and Acquisition actions, 
reputation and long-term market positioning. Motherson’s 
acquisition strategy is customer-driven and has a strong 
team to evaluate and strategisethe acquisition process. 
Specific risks monitored under this category include 
Reputational Risk, Continuous pressure from OEMs to 
reduce prices, Reliance on few customer

s or a single market 
and the ability to respond to future growth, industry trends 
and preferences. In addition, our inability to identify and 
adapt to evolving industry trends, new technology and 
preferences and develop new products to meet our 
customers’ demands may adversely aﬀect our business. 
These risks are assessed against material topics including 
Corporate Governance and Strategy, Business Ethics and 
Anti Corruption and Risk and Opportunity Management.
2.
Operating Risks: The Operating Risks can arise from 
internal factors and/or external factors. Further, the 
operating risks include the following:
(a)
Internal Factors:
•
Sourcing and supplies for changes in raw 
material prices; shortage of raw materials and 
components; dependence on single or few 
suppliers for procurement; and energy availability 
and pricing;
•
Revenue risks including continuous pressure 
from OEMs to reduce prices; reliance on single 
customer / market; and increased directed 
sourcing and multi-supplier sourcing by OEMs;
•
Quality and Product liability;
•
Risk emanating from the internal re-organisation 
or re-location of manufacturing operations, 
including managing new large programmes and 
production ramp-ups;
•
Managing Manufacturing capacities;
•
Logistics Management;
•
Attraction, Development and Retention of 
People, including the impact of significant rises 
in minimum wages across geographies; and
•
Processes – Internal controls and effective 
training of employees.

3.
Financial and Accounting Risks: This includes risks in 
terms of capital structure, forex risks such as currency risks, 
interest rate risks as well as financial obligations including 
liquidity and other obligations under financing 
arrangements. Additional risks monitored include significant 
fluctuations in raw material prices, under-recovery of costs 
due to lower volumes or model discontinuation, contingent

strategy, the Group has facilities across the globe, close to 
customer, minimising currency risks. The Company and its

Commercial Papers additional Equity Shares and

4.
Sustainability Risks: With globally distributed operations, 
the Group faces physical risks to life and property due to 
extreme weather events; transition risks resulting from 
disruptions in the market and emerging regulations; 
disruptions to operations due to water scarcity, e-waste and 
solid waste regulations. It also faces significant reputational 
risks, particularly from social and governance issues such as 
human rights, value chain due diligence etc. Specific risks 
identified under this category include Act of God / Natural 
factors and Environment, Social Policy and Governance 
risks. These are mapped against material topics including 
Climate Change Adaptation, Climate and Environmental 
Action (Mitigation), Health and Safety, and C

orporate 
Governance and Strategy.
5.
Regulatory and Compliance Risks: This includes risks with 
respect to multiple jurisdiction laws and regulations, 
intellectual property, patents, tax compliance and transfer 
pricing. Motherson, as a global organisation, has to comply 
with a complex regulatory landscape across multiple 
jurisdictions, covering areas such as Employment and 
Labour, Taxation, Foreign Exchange and Export Control, 
Sanctions restrictions, Environment, Health and Safety, Anti-
Bribery and Anti-Corruption, Data Privacy and so on. The 
laws and regulations are continuously evolving, increasing in 
number and complexity. This has resulted in greater 
compliance risk and cost of compliance for the Group. As a 
mitigation tool, Motherson has also formulated a Code of 
Conduct for best ethical practices and other best practices 
as part of Global Policies applicable to all associates of the 
Motherson Group on a uniform basis. The Group conducts 
training(s) and aﬀirmation programmes for its associates. 
For the management of Regulatory and Compliance Risk, 
Motherson has legal and compliance experts appointed in 
various jurisdictions who support and provide guidance to 
oﬀicers ensuring compliances in various plants and other 
locations. Further, Regional Chairman Offices (RCOs) in 
diﬀerent regions adopt best practices to mitigate the risks 
from a regulatory perspective. Motherson as a global 
organisation is also committed to upholding the highest 
standards of corporate governance and ethical values, as 
the group believes that strong governance is the foundation 
of a sustainable and resilient organisation.
6.

exposed to changes in the geopolitical environment, as well 
as external factors including but not limited to trade 
tensions, localisation, wars, natural disasters etc. Geo-
political, geo-economical and social risks are monitored as a 
distinct risk category, given their potential to a

ﬀect sourcing, 
logistics, order fulfilment and overall financial performance. 
Recent conflicts / wars have shown us that geopolitical 
tensions could erupt at any time causing major disruption 
and that could go on indefinitely. We continue to closely 
monitor and respond to global developments that may pose 
challenges on sourcing, order fulfilment, turnaround time 
and our bottom line, by timely implementation of mitigation 
plans, as necessary in this regard.

As a global organization with operations across 47 countries, the

Group maintains a robust internal control framework designed to 
safeguard assets, ensure the reliability of financial and operational 
reporting, enhance operational efficiency, and promote 
compliance with applicable laws, regulations, and internal policies.
Framework and Governance Architecture
The Company’s internal control framework is commensurate with 
the size, scale, and complexity of its operations and is aligned with 
the requirements of the Companies Act, 2013, the SEBI (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, and 
globally accepted governance standards. The framework 
comprises entity-level controls, process-level controls, information 
technology controls, and period-end financial reporting controls.
Key components of the framework include Enterprise Risk 
Management, Legal Compliance Management, Internal Audit, 
Code of Conduct, Ethics Framework, Vigil Mechanism/ Whistle-
Blower Policy established pursuant to Section 177(9) and (10) of 
the Companies Act, 2013, and anti-fraud controls. Together, these 
mechanisms reinforce effective governance, accountability, 
transparency, and ethical business conduct across the 
organization.
The internal control framework is designed to provide reasonable 
assurance regarding:
(a)
Accuracy, completeness, and authorization of transactions;
(b)
Reliability and integrity of financial and operational reporting;
(c)
Compliance with applicable laws, regulations, and internal 
policies;
(d)
Eﬀicient utilization of resources and safeguarding of assets; 
and
(e)
Identification, assessment, and mitigation of key business 
risks.
The Group leverages integrated Enterprise Resource Planning, 
Supplier Relationship Management, and Customer Relationship 
Management platforms to facilitate standardized processes, real-
time monitoring, and seamless information flow across its global 
operations. Given its highly interconnected digital environment, 
information security and cybersecurity remain key foc

us areas 
and are subject to periodic assessments by internal specialists, 
independent experts, and statutory auditors.
For entities acquired through business combinations, mergers, 
and amalgamations during the year, the Group undertakes a 
comprehensive assessment of the existing control environment 
and progressively aligns internal controls with the Motherson 
Governance and Control Framework to ensure consistency in risk 
management and control practices across the Group.
Internal Audit and Monitoring
The Group has an independent and multidisciplinary Internal 
Audit function that adopts a risk-based approach to evaluate the 
adequacy and eﬀectiveness of internal controls, governance 
processes, and risk management practices. The Internal Audit 
function periodically assesses the design and operating 
eﬀectiveness of controls and reviews compliance with established 
policies and procedures.
The Group continues to strengthen its assurance capabilities 
through advanced audit methodologies, data analytics, and 
technology-enabled monitoring tools, enhancing audit coverage, 
risk identification, and overall control eﬀectiveness. Specialized 
external experts are engaged periodically to review critical areas 
such as information security, quality management, transfer 
pricing, and regulatory compliance.
The Group operates through twelve Business Verticals supported 
by five Regional Chairman Oﬀices across South Asia, Southeast 
Asia, Europe, Americas and China region(s). Internal audit reports 
from all regions are presented to the Audit Committee, ensuring 
consistent oversight and independent review of significant 
observations, remediation measures, and emerging risks across 
the global organization.
The Audit Committee, comprising a majority of Independent 
Directors and chaired by an Independent Director, oversees the 
eﬀectiveness of the Company’s internal control environment, risk 
management framework, and implementation of audit 
recommendations. Signific

ant audit findings, management 
responses, and corrective action plans are reviewed periodically 
by the Audit Committee. The Audit Committee also reviews the 
functioning of the Vigil Mechanism in accordance with Regulation 
22 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015.
The Risk Management Committee, constituted in compliance 
with Regulation 21 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015, oversees the Enterprise Risk 
Management framework and reviews the risk profile of the Group

What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine basis by the 
entity?
At Motherson, we adopt a proactive, systematic, and structured approach to the identification and assessment of work 
related hazards and occupational health and safety risks. A combination of routine and non routine processes is employed 
to ensure a comprehensive evaluation of potential hazards across operations.
Designated and trained personnel cond

uct regular safety inspection walks to identify existing and potential workplace 
hazards. These inspections support ongoing monitoring of compliance with safety requirements and enable early 
identification of emerging risks. Periodic and task based risk assessments are conducted across activities, processes, and 
operational areas to systematically evaluate hazards and determine appropriate control measures.
Monthly and quarterly audits are undertaken to review hazard identification and risk assessment inputs, evaluate the 
eﬀectiveness of existing controls, and identify opportunities for improvement. Audit outcomes are reviewed by management 
as part of the continual improvement process. From an equipment and plant perspective, the Company prioritizes planned 
and preventive maintenance programs. These programs are designed to minimize risks arising from equipment malfunction, 
degradation, or failure.
Risk assessments are conducted prior to commencement of work, production start ups, or non routine activities to identify 
specific hazards and ensure appropriate controls are in place before execution.
The Company emphasizes active participation of employees in hazard identification and risk management. Ongoing 
training, awareness programs, and monitoring processes are deployed, with continuous improvement measured through 
qualitative and quantitative objectives, targets, and action plans aligned with international standards and local requirements.
In the event of an incident, a structured investigation process is followed, including escalation to appropriate management 
levels. Investigations focus on root cause analysis, with corrective and preventive actions implemented to mitigate future 
risks and prevent recurrence.
Overall, the Company is committed to continuous hazard and risk identification and assessment, supported by employee 
involvement, leadership oversight, and structured improvement mechanisms, thereby promoting a safe and healthy working 
enviro

nment across its operations.

Executive Summary of Impact Assessment Report
INTRODUCTION
Samvardhana Motherson International Limited ("SAMIL"), through its Water, Sanitation, Hygiene and Education ("WASHE") programme, 
has undertaken targeted interventions to impro

ve infrastructure, sanitation, and learning environments in government schools located 
near its manufacturing operations. The programme responds to persistent challenges faced by government schools-particularly in rural 
and peri-urban areas-where inadequate WASH facilities, poor classroom conditions, and limited access to digital learning tools adversely 
aﬀect student comfort, participation, and overall educational experience.
This impact assessment, covers WASHE interventions implemented between the years from 2022 to 2024 across selected government 
schools in Greater Noida (Uttar Pradesh) and Haryana. The assessment examines programme performance using the OECD-DAC 
evaluation framework. A mixed-methods methodology was adopted, combining quantitative surveys of students and teachers, focus 
group discussions, and a review of programme documentation.
PROGRAMME COVERAGE AND INTERVENTIONS
The WASHE programme delivered a comprehensive set of interventions structured around three thematic pillars:
Infrastructure and WASH: Renovation and construction of sanitation facilities, provision of water access, installation of rainwater 
harvesting systems, Kota stone flooring in classrooms and corridors, roof maintenance and waterproofing, whitewashing, and related 
civil works aimed at improving safety, hygiene, and durability of school infrastructure.
Furniture and Learning Environment: Provision of desks and benches to replace floor seating, installation of lights and fans to improve 
classroom comfort, and BaLA (Building as Learning Aid) paintings to create engaging, child-friendly spaces.
Digital Education: Installation of smart classrooms equipped with digital boards and supporting hardware, accompanied by a three-
year Annual Maintenance Contract (AMC). In addition to day schools, the programme supported a Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya 
(KGBV) Girls' Hostel, where targeted upgrades were undertaken to address sanitation, water management, structural deficiencies, a

nd 
lack of personal storage for resident students.
KEY FINDINGS
Relevance: The programme was found to be highly relevant to the needs of schools. A large majority of teachers and school management 
indicated that the interventions directly addressed critical infrastructure gaps that had persisted over several years. Students also 
reported visible improvements in cleanliness, comfort, and classroom conditions. The programme aligns well with national initiatives 
such as Swachh Vidyalaya and Samagra Shiksha, while also responding to site-specific challenges, including waterlogging in low-lying 
campuses.
Eﬀectiveness: The WASHE interventions were largely eﬀective in achieving their intended outputs. Over 90% of teachers reported 
that renovated toilets were fully functional, with water available in or near the facilities. Classroom infrastructure upgrades resulted in 
improved lighting, ventilation, and seating arrangements. Around two-thirds of teachers reported that student participation in classroom 
activities improved following the interventions, which they attributed to tangible changes in the learning environment, particularly the 
shift from floor seating to desks and benches, smoother flooring and improved ventilation.
Smart classrooms emerged as a key output. At the time of assessment, 80% of teachers reported that smart classrooms were functional 
and being used, while 20% indicated non-functionality primarily due to the expiry of AMC-linked service or subscription packages, rather 
than equipment failure. In schools where smart classrooms remained operational, 36% of teachers reported daily use, with an additional 
24% indicating frequent use.
Eﬀiciency: The programme demonstrated strong time eﬀiciency, with 96% of respondents indicating that interventions were completed 
within planned timelines. Minor delays were reported in a small number of cases, largely due to external factors such as site-specific 
constraints and temporary regulatory measures, in

cluding restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP). Clear assignment 
of maintenance responsibilityto schools facilitated orderly handover of assets.
Impact: The assessment identifies positive, emerging impacts on school functioning and student experience. Majority of students 
reported that classrooms and facilities were better than before, particularly noting improvements in seating, sanitation, water access 
and digital learning tools. Qualitative feedback from teachers and school management suggests improved attendance and retention 
owing to a more conducive classroom environment.

In schools where rainwater harvesting systems and walking pathways were constructed, stakeholders reported that chronic 
waterlogging during the monsoon season was resolved, significantly improving safety and access to classrooms. At the KGBV Girls' 
Hostel, interventions led to substantial improvements in hygiene, water management, structural safety, and personal storage, enhancing 
students' dignity, privacy and daily living conditions.
Coherence: The WASHE programme demonstrates strong coherence with the broader education and WASH ecosystem. Qualitative 
evidence indicates that, at the time of programme initiation, most intervention schools had received limited or no prior external 
infrastructure support and were in a highly deteriorated condition. Any subsequent contributions from other corporates occurred 
later and did not overlap with WASHE activities. The programme therefore functioned as a gap-filling intervention, complementing 
government eﬀorts rather than duplicating them.
Sustainability: While 96% of respondents expressed confidence that improvements are likely to be sustained, the assessment identified 
notable sustainability risks. Schools rely on government maintenance grants typically ranging from INR 50,000 to INR 75,000 per 
year, which stakeholders reported as insuﬀicient to cover recurring costs for

sanitation facilities, water systems, and digitally enabled 
infrastructure.Instances of non-functional rainwater harvesting units due to lack of regular maintenance, and smart classrooms becoming 
inoperative following AMC expiry, highlight constraints within existing government systems for post-installation servicing and renewal.
CONCLUSION
Overall, the assessment concludes that the WASHE programme has been well-targeted, eﬀectively implemented, and responsive to 
the foundational infrastructure and learning needs of government schools. By addressing sanitation, physical learning conditions, and 
access to digital tools in an integrated manner, the programme has contributed to measurable improvements in school environments 
and student experience. Strengthening government led mechanisms for maintenance financing, service renewal, and addressing 
remaining infrastructure gaps shall be critical to sustaining and deepening these gains in future phases.

OECD-DAC Framework
This study has deployed the OECD-DAC framework evaluation criteria throughout the impact evaluation process to develop a qualitative 
understanding of the impact created, stakeholder perceptions, and sustenance of the change envisioned under the project.
The OECD DAC Network on Devel

opment Evaluation (EvalNet) has defined six evaluation criteria – relevance, coherence, eﬀectiveness, 
eﬀiciency, impact and sustainability. These criteria are intended to guide evaluations. These have been in use since 1991 and were refined 
in 2019 to improve the quality and usefulness of evaluation and further strengthen the contribution of the evaluation itself to sustainable 
development.

Remuneration Policy
The Company has adopted a remuneration policy in consonance 
with the industry practices and rewards good performance of the 
employees of the Company. The policy ensures equality, fairness 
and consistency in rewarding the employees on the basis of 
performance against set objectives and the performance of the 
individuals measured through the annual appraisal process.
Remuneration policy of the Company is designed to create a high- 
performance culture. It enables the Company to attract, retain 
and motivate employees to achieve results. Our business model 
promotes customer centricity and requires employee mobility to 
address project needs.
The Compan

y pays remuneration by way of salary, benefits, 
perquisites and allowances to its Executive Director. Annual 
increments 
are 
recommended 
by 
the 
Nomination 
and 
Remuneration Committee within the salary scale approved by 
Members and the Board. Annual increments are eﬀective April 1 
of each year.
The Board of Directors, inter-alia, decides commission payable 
to the Independent Directors out of the profits for respective 
financial year and within ceilings prescribed under the Companies 
Act, 2013, based on evaluation process and considering criteria, 
such as, performance of the Company.
Performance Evaluation criteria for Independent Directors 
The performance of the Directors including the Independent 
Directors is evaluated on the basis of the criteria specified as per 
the Guidance Note on Board Evaluation issued by the Securities 
and Exchange Board of India (“SEBI”) with the aim to improve 
the eﬀectiveness of the Board and the Committees. The said 
criteria provides certain parameters like qualification, experience, 
knowledge and competencies, fulfilment of functions, ability to 
function as a team, initiative, commitment and their participation 
and contribution at the Board meetings and Committee meetings, 
independence from the Company and other Directors, providing 
independent views and judgement and expertise to provide 
feedback and guidance to top management on business strategy, 
governance, risk, understanding of the organization’s strategy, 
internal and external environment.
In order to strengthen the board evaluation process and ensure 
good corporate governance, the Company has developed an 
in-house transparent software for the Board Evaluation. The said 
Report on Corporate Governance (Contd.)
software enabled directors to complete the Board Evaluation 
process digitally, on an anonymous basis.
The process for Board Evaluation for financial year 2025-26 was open 
for responses by the Directors from April 22, 2026 to May 14, 2026. 
The

consolidated responses were made available to the Chairperson 
of Nomination and Remuneration Committee for review by the 
Board of Directors.

Global Sustainability Committee
SEBI vide its notification dated May 10, 2021 has introduced new reporting requirements for the Business Responsibility and 
Sustainability Report (BRSR). BRSR seeks disclosures from listed entities on their performance against nine principles of the 
‘National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct’ and reporting under each principle is divided into essential and leadership
indicators. BRSR shall be applicable to the top 1000 listed entities (by market capitalization) from financial year 2023 –24.
The United Nations Global Compact (“UNGC”) provides a principle-based framework for businesses, stating Ten Principles for 
human rights, labor, environment and an

ti- corruption. The United Nations (UN) has developed 17 Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs) for achieving transformational change across the globe.
In pursuance of the above, the Board of Directors in its meeting held on June 2, 2021 constituted Global Sustainability Committee. 
The Board of Directors in its meeting has also approved for participation in UNGC. The said Committee, subject to the overall 
superintendence, control and direction of the Board, is responsible for driving the sustainability goals as prescribed by SEBI and by 
UN for adoption on voluntary basis.
The Committee met four (4) times, i.e. on (1) April 16, 2025; (2) July 23, 2025; (3) October 16, 2025 and (4) January 14, 2026 during 
the financial year 2025-26 and requisite quorum was present at such Committee meetings.

Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with Reference to

A company’s internal financial controls with reference to 
standalone financial statements is a process designed to provide 
reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial 
reporting and the preparation of

financial statements for external

principles. A company’s internal financial controls with reference 
to standalone financial statements includes those policies and 
procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in 
reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions 
and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide 
reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary 
to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with 
generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and 
expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance 
with authorisations of management and directors of the company; 
and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or 
timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of 
the company’s assets that could have a material eﬀect on the 
financial statements.

original equipment manufacturers. The address of its registered oﬀice is Unit 705, C Wing, ONE BKC, G Block, Bandra Kurla 
Complex, Bandra East, Mumbai, Maharashtra. The Company is a public limited company and is listed in the Bombay Stock 
Exchange and National Stock Exchange.
The standalone financial statements were authorised for issue in accordance with a resolution of the Board of directors on May 20, 
2026.
2.1
Material accounting policies
(a)
Basis of preparation
The financial statements of the Company have been prepared in accordance with Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) 
notified under the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015 (as amended from time to time) and presentation 
requirements of Division II of Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013, (Ind AS compliant Schedule III), as applicable to the 
financial statement.
The financial statements have been prepared on a historical cost basis, except for the following assets and liabilities which 
have been measured at fair value:
•
Derivative financial instruments, refer note 37
•
Certain financial assets and liabilities measured at fair value (refer note 1 below for accounting policy regarding financial 
instruments)
•
Defined benefit pension plans – plan assets measured at fair value, refer note 21
In addition, the carrying values of recognised assets and liabilities designated as hedged items in fair value hedges that 
would otherwise be carried at amortised cost are adjusted to record changes in the fair values attributable to the risks that 
are being hedged

in eﬀective hedge relationships. The financial statements are presented in INR, and all values are rounded 
to the nearest millions (INR 000,000), except when otherwise indicated.
The Company segregates assets and liabilities into current and non-current categories for presentation in the balance sheet 
after considering its normal operating cycle and other criteria set out in Ind AS 1, “Presentation of Financial Statements”. For 
this purpose, current assets and liabilities include the current portion of non-current assets and liabilities respectively. 
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are always classified as non-current.
The operating cycle is the time between the acquisition of assets for processing and their realization in cash and cash 
equivalents. The Company has identified period up to twelve months as its operating cycle.
The Company has prepared the standalone financial statements on the basis that it will continue to operate as a going 
concern.
(b)
New and amended standards
a)
The Company applied for the first-time certain standards and amendments, which are eﬀective for annual periods 
beginning on or after 1 April 2025. The Company has not early adopted any standard, interpretation or amendment 
that has been issued but is not yet eﬀective.

(i)
Amendments to Ind AS 21 - Lack of exchangeability
The Ministry of Corporate Aﬀairs (MCA) notified the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Amendment Rules, 
2025, which amend Ind AS 21, The Eﬀects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates to specify how an entity should 
assess whether a currency is exchangeable and how it should determine a spot exchange rate when exchangeability is 
lacking. The amendments also require disclosure of information that enables users of its financial statements to 
understand how the currency not being exchangeable into the other currency a

ﬀects, or is expected to aﬀect, the 
entity’s financial performance, financial position and cash flows.
The amendments are eﬀective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025. When applying the 
amendments, an entity cannot restate comparative information.
The amendments do not have a material impact on the Company’s financial statements.
(ii)
Amendments to Ind AS 1 - Classification of Liabilities as Current or Non-current and Non-current Liabilities with 
Covenants
In August 2025, the MCA notified amendments to paragraphs 69 to 76 of Ind AS 1 to specify the requirements for 
classifying liabilities as current or non-current. The amendments clarify:
•
What is meant by a right to defer settlement
•
That a right to defer must exist at the end of the reporting period
•
That classification is unaﬀected by the likelihood that an entity will exercise its deferral right
•
That only if an embedded derivative in a convertible liability is itself an equity instrument would the terms of a 
liability not impact its classification In addition, a requirement has been introduced to require disclosure when a 
liability arising from a loan agreement is classified as non-current and the entity’s right to defer settlement is 
contingent on compliance with future covenants within twelve months.
If there is a breach of a material covenant of a long term loan arrangement on or before the end of the reporting 
period, resulting in the liability becoming payable on demand as at the reporting date, and the lender agrees—after the 
reporting period but before the financial statements are approved for issue—not to demand repayment for at least 12 
months as a consequence of the breach, this shall be treated as an adjusting event. Accordingly, the entity is not 
required to classify the liability as current.
The amendments are eﬀective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025 retrospectively in 
accordance with Ind AS 8.
The amendments have resulted

in additional disclosures in Note 17 but have not had an impact on the classification of 
Company’s liabilities.
(iii)
Amendments to Ind AS 7 and Ind AS 107 - Supplier Finance Arrangements
In August 2025, the MCA notified amendments to Ind AS 7 Statement of Cash Flows and Ind AS 107 Financial 
Instruments: Disclosures to clarify the characteristics of supplier finance arrangements and require additional 
disclosure of such arrangements. The disclosure requirements in the amendments are intended to assist users of 
financial statements in understanding the eﬀects of supplier finance arrangements on an entity’s liabilities, cash flows 
and exposure to liquidity risk.
As a result of implementing the amendments, the Company has provided additional disclosures about its supplier 
finance arrangement.

Revenue from contracts with customers
Revenue from contracts with customers is recognised when control of the goods or services are transferred to the customer 
at an amount that reflects the consideration to which the Company expects to be entitled in exchange for those goods or 
services. The Company has generally concluded that it is the principal in its revenue arrangements, except for the agency 
services below, because it typically controls the goods or services before transferring them to the customer.

Revenue from sale of components is recognised at the point in time when control of the asset is transferred to the customer,

Variable consideration
If the consideration in a contract includes a variable amount, the Company estimates the amount of consideration to which 
it will be entitled in exchange for transferring the goods to the customer. The variable consideration is estimated at contract 
inception and constrained until it is highly probable that a significant revenue reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue 
recognised will not occur when the associated uncertainty with the variable consideration is subsequently resolved.
Volume rebates
The Company applies the most likely amount method or the expected value method

to estimate the variable consideration 
in the contract. The selected method that best predicts the amount of variable consideration is primarily driven by the 
number of volume thresholds contained in the contract. The most likely amount is used for those contracts with a single 
volume threshold, while the expected value method is used for those with more than one volume threshold. The Company 
then applies the requirements on constraining estimates in order to determine the amount of variable consideration that can 
be included in the transaction price and recognised as revenue. A refund liability is recognised for the expected future 
rebates (i.e., the amount not included in the transaction price).

Trade Receivables
Trade receivables are amounts due from customers for goods sold or services performed in the ordinary course of business. 
They are generally due for settlement within one year and therefore are all classified as current. Where the settlement is due 
after one year, they are classified as non-current. Trade receivables are recognised initially at the amount of consideration 
that is unconditional unless they contain significant financing components, when they are recognised at fair value. The 
Company holds the trade receivables with the objective to collect the contractual cash flows and therefore measures them 
subsequently at amortised cost using the eﬀective interest method. Trade receivables are disclosed in Note 45.
Contract Assets
A contract asset is the entity’s right to consideration in exchange for goods or services that the entity has transferred to the 
customer. A contract asset is recognised where receipt of consideration is conditional on successful completion of another 
performance obligation. The impairment of contract assets is measured, presented and disclosed on the same basis as 
trade receivables. The Company’s contract assets are disclosed in Note 45 as unbilled revenue.
Contract Liabilities
A contract liability is the obligation to transfer goods or services to a customer for which the Company has received 
consideration (or an amount of consideration is due) from the customer. If a customer pays consideration before the 
Company transfers goods or services to the customer, a contract liability is recognised when the payment is made or the 
payment is due (whichever is earlier). Contract liabilities are recognised as revenue when the Company performs under the 
contract. Contract Liabilities are disclosed in Note 45 as Advances received from customers.
Impairment
An impair

ment is recognised to the extent that the carrying amount of receivable or asset relating to contracts with 
customers (a) the remaining amount of consideration that the Company expects to receive in exchange for the goods or 
services to which such asset relates; less (b) the costs that relate directly to providing those goods or services and that have 
not been recognised as expenses.
(e)
Other income
Interest
Interest is recognised using the eﬀective interest rate (EIR) method, as income for the period in which it occurs. EIR is the rate 
that exactly discounts the estimated future cash payments or receipts over the expected life of the financial instrument to 
the gross carrying amount of the financial asset or to the amortised cost of a financial liability. When calculating the eﬀective 
interest rate, the Company estimates the expected cash flows by considering all the contractual terms of the financial 
instrument (for example, prepayment, extension, call and similar options) but does not consider the expected credit losses.
Dividend
Dividend income is recognised when the right to receive dividend is established, which is generally when shareholders 
approve the dividend. In case of interim dividend, it is recognised as receivable when it is declared by the Board of respective 
investee companies.
Duty drawback and export incentives
Income from duty drawback and export incentives is recognized on an accrual basis.

Impairment of non-financial assets
The Company assesses, at each reporting date, whether there is an indication that an asset may be impaired. If any indication 
exists, or when annual impairment testing for an asset is required, the Company estimates the asset’s recoverable amount. 
An asset’s recoverable amount is the higher of an asset’s or cash-generating unit’s (CGU) fair value less costs of disposal and 
its value in use. Recoverable amount is determined

for an individual asset, unless the asset does not generate cash inflows 
that are largely independent of those from other assets or groups of assets. When the carrying amount of an asset or CGU 
exceeds its recoverable amount, the asset is considered impaired and is written down to its recoverable amount.
In assessing value in use, the estimated future cash flows are discounted to their present value using a pre-tax discount rate 
that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the asset. In determining fair 
value less costs of disposal, recent market transactions are taken into account. If no such transactions can be identified, an 
appropriate valuation model is used. These calculations are corroborated by valuation multiples, quoted share prices for 
publicly traded companies or other available fair value indicators.
The Company bases its impairment calculation on detailed budgets and forecast calculations, which are prepared separately 
for each of the Company’s CGUs to which the individual assets are allocated. These budgets and forecast calculations 
generally cover a period of five years. For longer periods, a long-term growth rate is calculated and applied to project future 
cash flows after the fifth year. To estimate cash flow projections beyond periods covered by the most recent budgets/
forecasts, the Company extrapolates cash flow projections in the budget using a steady or declining growth rate for 
subsequent years, unless an increasing rate can be justified. In any case, this growth rate does not exceed the long-term 
average growth rate for the products, industries, or country or countries in which the entity operates, or for the market in 
which the asset is used. Impairment losses including impairment on inventories, are recognised in the statement of profit 
and loss
For assets including goodwill, an assessment is made at each reporting date to determine whether there is an indication that 
previou

sly recognised impairment losses no longer exist or have decreased. If such indication exists, the Company estimates 
the asset’s or CGU’s recoverable amount. A previously recognised impairment loss is reversed only if there has been a 
change in the assumptions used to determine the asset’s recoverable amount since the last impairment loss was recognised. 
The reversal is limited so that the carrying amount of the asset does not exceed its recoverable amount, nor exceed the 
carrying amount that would have been determined, net of depreciation, had no impairment loss been recognised for the 
asset in prior years. Such reversal is recognised in the statement of profit and loss.
